lesson.title: Splitting Power Between Two Governments at Once
lesson.summary: Federalism, the system the Constitutional Convention built for dividing authority between national and state governments, tried to solve the opposite failures of the too-weak Articles of Confederation and a feared too-strong national government.
lesson.body:
Delegates arriving in Philadelphia in 1787 were caught between two experiences they wanted to avoid repeating. They had just spent years watching the Articles of Confederation fail because it gave states nearly all the power and left the national government too weak to tax, regulate trade, or respond to crises like Shays' Rebellion. But most delegates, along with the broader public they represented, also remembered a distant British government that had taxed and governed the colonies without their consent, and they had no interest in simply recreating an all-powerful national authority in its place.

The system that emerged from the convention, built on the framework the Great Compromise had already established for representation, tried to thread that needle by dividing power between two levels of government rather than concentrating it in one. The national government received specific, enumerated powers, spelled out in the Constitution itself, including the power to coin money, declare war, regulate interstate and foreign commerce, and raise an army. States retained broad authority over matters like education, local law enforcement, and most of what touched daily life, powers that were not listed simply because the framers assumed states would keep whatever they had not explicitly handed over.

Some powers, like the ability to levy taxes or maintain courts, belonged to both levels of government simultaneously, a category later scholars would call concurrent powers. To settle disputes between state and national law, the framers included the Supremacy Clause in Article VI, which established that the Constitution and federal laws made under it would prevail whenever they genuinely conflicted with state law.

This arrangement differed sharply from the confederation model the Articles had used, where states retained nearly all meaningful power and the national government existed largely at their sufferance. It also differed from a unitary system, common in many other countries, where a central government holds all authority and merely delegates administrative tasks to local units that it can revoke at will. Federalism instead created two genuinely independent sources of governmental authority, each deriving its power directly from the people rather than from the other.

James Madison would go on to defend this structure at length in the essays that came to be known as the Federalist Papers, arguing that splitting power between national and state governments, and then splitting national power further among three branches, gave citizens a double layer of protection against any single government growing too dominant. Not every delegate was convinced the balance was struck correctly, and that very disagreement would soon define the ratification debate between the Constitution's supporters and its critics.
